title: Dependency Injection & Designing for Testability
summary: How to structure object construction so dependencies are supplied, not hand-built, so production and test code can substitute them freely.

slides.markdown:
A class that does `new EmailService()` inside its own constructor has welded itself to one implementation forever — you can't swap it for a mock in a test, or a different provider in production, without editing that class's source.

**Dependency injection** flips this: an object receives its dependencies from outside instead of constructing them itself. Think of a lamp with a replaceable bulb versus one with the bulb soldered in — the socket is the seam that makes swapping possible.

This topic covers the three ways to inject, when a DI container earns its keep, and the seam that turns hard-wired code into code you can actually test.

slides.sectionTitle: Why `new` inside a class is a design smell
slides.markdown:
When a class calls `new EmailService()` or `new PostgresRepository()` inside its own constructor or methods, it has **hard-wired** itself to one concrete implementation. The class now owns two jobs: doing its actual work, and deciding how to build its dependencies.

The cost shows up the moment you need a different context — writing a unit test, swapping providers, or running against a staging database. You can't intercept that `new` call from outside, so the only way to change behavior is to edit the class's source, recompile, and redeploy.

The smell isn't `new` itself — it's `new` for something the *caller*, not the class, should get to decide.

**Dependency injection (DI)** means an object receives its dependencies from the outside — passed in — instead of constructing them itself. The object declares what it needs; something else (a caller, a factory, a container) decides what concrete thing to hand over.

Concretely: instead of a class that builds `private repo = new PostgresRepository()` internally, you write a constructor that takes `repo: Repository` as a parameter, and let whoever creates the object choose which implementation to pass.

The payoff is substitution: production code passes the real `PostgresRepository`; a test passes an in-memory fake. The class itself never changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Constructor injection vs setter/property injection vs method injection
slides.markdown:
Where a dependency gets injected changes what guarantees you get. All three exist in real codebases — the choice is about when the dependency is known and whether it can change later.

| | Constructor injection | Setter/property injection | Method injection |
|---|---|---|---|
| When supplied | Once, at construction | After construction, any time | Per call, as a parameter |
| Can it be missing? | No — object is invalid without it | Yes, until someone calls the setter | No, but scoped to one call |
| Best for | Required, stable dependencies | Optional dependencies, framework-managed lifecycles | A dependency that varies per operation (e.g. current user) |

**How to decide:** default to constructor injection — it makes "this object cannot exist without its dependencies" a compile-time guarantee. Reach for setter or method injection only when the dependency is genuinely optional or varies per call.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a class graph before and after extracting seams
slides.markdown:
![OrderService hard-wired to PostgresRepository, versus OrderService depending on a Repository seam that both PostgresRepository and InMemoryRepository implement](assets/di-seam.svg)

Before: `OrderService` holds a direct reference to `PostgresRepository` — one box wired straight into another, no room to substitute.

After: `OrderService` depends on a `Repository` interface instead. `PostgresRepository` and an `InMemoryRepository` used in tests both implement it. The **seam** is that interface boundary — the exact point where you can swap what's plugged in without touching `OrderService`.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: refactoring a hard-wired EmailService into a constructor-injected dependency
Injecting an abstraction, not a concrete class
slides.markdown:
Constructor injection alone doesn't guarantee testability — a constructor that takes `emailer: SmtpEmailService` is still injected, but it's injected as a *concrete class*, so a test still needs something that behaves like real SMTP.

The seam only appears when the constructor asks for an **interface** (or abstract class) instead: `constructor(private emailer: Emailer)`. Now any object satisfying that shape — the real SMTP client, a fake that records calls, a stub that always succeeds — can be passed in. This is the same idea system design calls the **Dependency Inversion Principle**: depend on an abstraction, not a concrete implementation.

Injection without abstraction is just moving the `new` call one level up — it doesn't buy you substitution.

A **DI container** (Spring, NestJS's injector, .NET's built-in container) scans your classes, works out the dependency graph, and constructs objects for you at startup. **Manual wiring** means you write the `new` calls yourself, usually in one composition-root function.

| | DI container | Manual wiring |
|---|---|---|
| Setup cost | Config or annotations, a learning curve | Zero — just function calls |
| Traceability | Wiring is implicit, resolved at runtime | Wiring is explicit, one file to read |
| Scales to | Large graphs, scoped lifecycles | Small-to-medium graphs |
| Debugging a wiring bug | Runtime error, sometimes cryptic | Compile error or an obvious missing argument |

**How to decide:** manual wiring wins for small services and libraries — you can read the whole graph in one file. Reach for a container once the graph is large enough that manual wiring becomes its own maintenance burden.

**Wrong belief:** "I've made everything injectable, so this class is well-designed."

**Why it's wrong:** a constructor with twelve injected dependencies is fully testable and still a bad design — it's almost certainly doing twelve jobs. DI removes the *technical* friction of hard-wiring, but it doesn't fix a class with too many responsibilities; it just makes the overloaded class easier to instantiate in a test.

**Correct model:** treat a growing constructor as a signal to split the class, the same way you'd treat a growing method. If you can't describe what a class does in one sentence without "and", injecting its dependencies isn't the fix — separating its responsibilities is.
